title: Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room
full_review:
It is a classic example of cruel irony that Enron, a company synonymous with covering
up the truth, would choose as its advertising slogan "Ask Why?"

In March 2001, Bethany McLean, a reporter from Fortune magazine, began to do just that.

A fascinating new documentary, "Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room" (Magnolia), based on the best-selling book of the same title that McLean co-wrote with Peter Elkind, follows her lead, asking who was responsible for the downfall of Enron.

Part probing study of corporate corruption, part Greek tragedy, the film by Emmy Award-winning director Alex Gibney chronicles the rise and collapse of the now-infamous energy giant, which before its demise was the seventh largest company in the nation.

The film analyzes the Darwinian mind-set that dominated the company's upper echelons and created what Gibney calls "a moral vacuum" which, through an insidious combination of murky ethics, avarice and blind hubris, precipitated one of the greatest corporate-fraud scandals in U.S. history, in which top Enron executives walked away with more than $1 billion while investors and employees lost everything.

While much of what is detailed -- including how Enron's hierarchy deceived shareholders and created the illusion of financial robustness -- may be lost on viewers without a business background, the story of Enron is, as McLean points out, about people, "not about complex numbers."

The documentary combines interviews with journalists, former employees and Wall Street insiders, archival news footage and re-enactments to craft a sobering portrait of arrogance and greed.

Catholic tradition holds that it was pride that caused the angels to fall. According to this film, it also seems to have had a hand in toppling some guys who were not as smart as they thought they were.

The film contains strip-club images involving nudity, a dramatized suicide and sporadic rough and crude language. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. It is not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
